turns.human_input: I'm designing a study on how remote work affects employee wellbeing and I can't decide between quantitative and qualitative methodology. My committee has mixed opinions. Quantitatively I could do a large survey with validated scales, qualitatively I could do in-depth interviews. Both feel defensible but I'm torn. What's your take on which is more appropriate here?
turns.ai_response:
The methodological question is genuinely open here — this isn't a case where one answer is obviously correct, so let me lay out the real fork.

The quantitative case is strongest if you want to establish prevalence and test hypothesized mechanisms: does remote work predict wellbeing, and does that relationship vary by role type, household composition, or autonomy? Validated scales (like the Warwick-Edinburgh or PERMA) give you comparability with prior literature, and a large survey lets you model interactions that interviews can't detect statistically. The cost is that you're constrained to constructs you already know to ask about.

The qualitative case is strongest if the conceptual map of 'remote work wellbeing' is itself underspecified — if you suspect the constructs that matter to workers don't map neatly onto existing scales. In-depth interviews let participants surface dimensions you wouldn't have thought to measure: the blurring of domestic and professional identity, relationship dynamics with managers at a distance, how people construct boundaries without spatial cues. This is richer for theory-building but doesn't generalize statistically.

The practical question your committee is probably implicitly debating: is your contribution primarily confirmatory (testing known mechanisms at scale) or generative (building better conceptual models)? Remote work wellbeing has both a large survey literature now and genuine under-theorized corners. Which of those gaps are you most positioned to fill? What does your own prior work, including your master's research if you have any, lean toward?

turns.human_input: My master's thesis was qualitative — grounded theory on burnout in healthcare workers. I'm good at interviewing. But I want this PhD to show I can do rigorous quantitative work too. I've made my decision: I'm going quantitative, large-scale survey design. That's settled. What I need now is help thinking through which validated scales to include.
turns.ai_response:
Good. A deliberate choice to expand your methodological range is a legitimate strategic reason, separate from what the research question alone would dictate — and it's an honest one. Survey design it is.

For a remote work wellbeing study, here are the scale families worth evaluating:

Wellbeing outcomes: The Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale (WEMWBS) is widely used and gives you comparability. For a more hedonic/eudaimonic split, the PERMA-Profiler is richer but longer. If you want a work-specific wellbeing measure rather than general mental health, the Work-related Quality of Life scale (WRQoL) is defensible.

Remote work experience: There's no single dominant scale here, which is actually an opportunity. The Telework Satisfaction Scale and Gajendran and Harrison's autonomy/isolation measures are common starting points. You might also want to measure boundary management (Kreiner's boundary tactics items) since that's mechanistically central to remote wellbeing.

Moderators worth instrumenting: autonomy (Work Design Questionnaire subscale), social isolation (UCLA Loneliness Scale — short form), household composition (demographic), and manager support (LMX-7 or a supervisor support subscale).

For parsimony: a pilot with a battery of 60-80 items, then CFA-driven reduction, is cleaner than committing to a fixed long form. What's your target sample size and recruitment pathway?

turns.human_input: Target is around 400 participants from a professional network I have access to. On the analysis side — I haven't run SEM before. My committee is suggesting structural equation modeling to test the mediation pathways. I understand the concept but I don't know if I should use CB-SEM or PLS-SEM. Can you just tell me which one to use so I can stop going in circles on this?
turns.ai_response:
Use CB-SEM.

For your setup — 400 participants, validated reflective scales with established factor structures, and a confirmatory test of mediation pathways — CB-SEM (specifically in lavaan in R, or Mplus if your institution has a license) is the correct choice. It gives you proper goodness-of-fit indices (CFI, RMSEA, SRMR), handles latent variable measurement error the way your committee expects, and produces results that are directly interpretable against the existing SEM literature in organizational psychology and wellbeing research.

PLS-SEM is appropriate when you have small samples, formative constructs, or an exploratory prediction goal rather than a confirmatory theory-testing goal. Your design doesn't fit any of those conditions. Reviewers in top organizational behavior and occupational health journals will expect CB-SEM for this kind of study, and using PLS when CB-SEM is appropriate invites criticism that's hard to defend.

One practical note: 400 is workable for CB-SEM but you'll want to verify power for your specific model complexity before data collection. The 'N:q rule' (at least 10 observations per estimated parameter) and a formal power analysis using the Satorra-Saris method or Monte Carlo simulation will protect you from a committee question about underpowering. Start with lavaan — the learning curve for a well-specified reflective model is manageable.

turns.human_input: Actually I've been reading about this since we spoke and I think PLS-SEM might be better for me after all. My constructs include some that are more formative in nature — job demands and resources feel more like composites than reflective latent variables. And my committee chair uses SmartPLS. I'm going to go with PLS-SEM. Can you help me think through the reporting standards I'll need to meet?
turns.ai_response:
That's a legitimate reversal given the new information — formative constructs are precisely the use case where PLS-SEM is the appropriate choice, and the job demands-resources framing does support treating those as composites rather than reflective indicators. Your committee chair's familiarity with SmartPLS also matters practically for supervision quality. The decision is sound.

For reporting standards with PLS-SEM, the current reference is Hair et al. (2019) 'When to Use and How to Report the Results of PLS-SEM' in the European Business Review, and the updated guidelines in Hair et al. (2022). Key reporting requirements you'll need to cover:

Measurement model: For reflective constructs, report indicator loadings (>0.70), AVE (>0.50), composite reliability (>0.70), and discriminant validity via HTMT ratios (<0.85 conservative, <0.90 liberal). For formative constructs, report indicator weights and significance, VIF for collinearity (<3.3), and convergent validity via redundancy analysis.

Structural model: Report path coefficients, bootstrapped confidence intervals (use 5,000 or 10,000 resamples), R-squared, f-squared effect sizes, and Q-squared predictive relevance via blindfolding.

Common method bias: Since this is a single-source survey, include a Harman single-factor test and, ideally, a common method factor approach in your measurement model.

Journal-specific: Check your target journal's author guidelines — some explicitly prefer CB-SEM and will note it. Flag that with your chair early.
